description: We are Mid-Chaotics, an FTC team passionate about robotics, engineering and innovation. Through FIRST, we have learned to turn ambitious ideas into practical solutions through creativity, teamwork, and critical thinking. Our name reflects our philosophy: innovation begins in chaos. We embrace challenges, question conventions, and turn obstacles into opportunities. We believe the future belongs to those who dare to think differently. And sometimes, a little chaos is exactly what innovation needs!
summary:
Since the beginning of space exploration, NASA has sent many spacecraft, landers, rovers, and scientific instruments beyond Earth. Some completed their missions and were left behind on the Moon or Mars, while others continue traveling through space or collecting valuable scientific data.

Our project, "Abandoned but Not Forgotten," tells the stories of these machines. Through examples such as the Lunar Roving Vehicle, Viking 1, Opportunity, Curiosity, and Voyager 1, we explore what they were designed to do, what they discovered, how long they operated, and what happened after their missions ended or changed.

Our goal is to help young space enthusiasts understand that these machines are more than pieces of old equipment. They represent years of human effort, scientific curiosity, and technological progress. Even when a mission ends, its discoveries continue to shape our understanding of the universe.
details:
Our project aims to make the history of space exploration more interesting and accessible to young people. Many people know about famous NASA missions, but they may not know what happens to spacecraft after their missions end.

By telling the stories of these machines, we want to show how much scientific knowledge can come from a single mission. We also hope to encourage students to become more curious about space, engineering, and science.

Most importantly, we want readers to understand that a spacecraft does not become meaningless when it stops working. The information it collected and the discoveries it made can remain valuable for generations.

Our project is a research-based storytelling article, so it does not require a programming language or a physical device.

We used online research, NASA's public information and mission archives, and artificial intelligence tools to support the research and writing process. We also compared information from different sources to develop a clear and engaging story for young readers.

Instead of presenting NASA's old spacecraft as simple lists of machines and technical facts, our project tells their stories.

We connect scientific achievements with the human effort behind each mission. By comparing spacecraft that worked for only a short time with others that operated for many years, and by including both completed and ongoing missions, we show different sides of space exploration.

This storytelling approach helps readers connect emotionally with the machines while learning about their scientific importance.

We considered the accuracy of the scientific information, the importance of each mission, and how understandable the article would be for school-age readers.

We selected examples from the Moon, Mars, and deep space to show the variety of NASA's missions. We also considered how long each spacecraft operated, what it discovered, and what happened after its mission ended.

Our main priority was to balance scientific accuracy with an engaging and easy-to-follow story.
